lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: Hi, and welcome. Before the Executive AI Academy, we want to give you something simple: a shared vocabulary.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: In the session, we'll follow one injured worker's claim, from the day it's reported to the day they're back at work.

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: And to talk about where AI fits on that journey, we all need to mean the same thing when we say "AI", "agent", or "human in the loop". So: about ten minutes, a dozen ideas. Let's start.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: When people say "AI", what do they actually mean?

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: It helps to think of three kinds. The first predicts. Predictive AI, or machine learning, learns patterns from past data to score or forecast. How complex is this claim likely to be? How many calls will we get next week?

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: The second reads and writes. Generative AI can summarize a thick claim file, answer questions about it, or draft a letter. That's what Copilot does today.

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: The third does the work. An agent doesn't just answer. It takes steps toward a goal.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Predicts, writes, does.

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: Exactly.

scenes.title: The large language model, and hallucination

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: So how does the "reads and writes" kind actually work?

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: Underneath is a large language model, or LLM. It does one thing: given the words so far, it predicts a likely next word. Then it does it again, and again.

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: Take "The worker hurt their…". The model scores every possible next word, like back, hand or knee, and picks a likely one.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: That sounds almost too simple.

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: It is simple. It's why these models are so fluent. But it's also why they can be wrong: a model produces what sounds likely, not what it has checked. A fluent, confident answer that isn't true is called a hallucination.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: So confident isn't the same as correct.

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: Right. Fluent is not the same as verified.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Then how can we trust what it says about a real claim?

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: We ground it. Before it answers, the system looks things up in trusted sources, like our policy manual, the claim file, or medical guidelines, and answers from those.

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: You'll hear this called RAG: retrieval-augmented generation. Retrieval: find the right documents. Augmented: add them to the question. Generation: write the answer from them.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And how would I know it did that?

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: Citations. A grounded answer shows where it came from, so a person can check it in seconds. Ask that of any AI tool: where did this answer come from, and can I see it?

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: You said agents do the work. How is that different from a chatbot?

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: A chatbot answers a question. An agent pursues a goal. The language model is the reasoning engine in the middle, and around it are five parts.

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: A goal: what "done" looks like, say, "get this claim ready for a decision". Instructions: the rules and limits it must follow. Tools: the systems it may use. Memory: what it knows about this claim so far. And a person, who approves and decides.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And when an agent goes wrong?

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: It's usually one of those five: a vague goal, a missing rule, too much access, out-of-date memory, or no person at the right moment.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: What does an agent actually do, step by step?

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: It runs a loop. Plan the next step. Act, usually by using a tool. Check the result. Then repeat until the goal is met.

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: Say it finds the doctor's note is missing. It plans to ask the clinic for it, drafts the request, and then stops, because sending anything outside WCB needs a person's approval.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: So it knows when to stop.

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: If we design it to: when the goal is met, when a rule says a person must approve, or when it's unsure. And because each step builds on the last, one early mistake can carry forward. You'll see that in the session.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: What decides what an agent can touch?

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: Tools are its hands, and it can only use what we connect it to. There are three levels: read, to look things up; draft, to prepare something for a person; and act, to change something in the world, like sending a letter or scheduling a payment.

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: The principle is least privilege: only the access the job needs. And like a new hire, every agent gets its own identity and a named human owner.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: So that's an IT setting?

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: IT sets it up. But what agents may do on WCB's behalf is a leadership decision.

scenes.title: The autonomy dial, and human in the loop

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: How much should an agent do on its own?

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: Picture a dial. At one end, it only suggests. Then it drafts for a person. Then it acts with approval. Then it acts and reports afterwards. At the far end, it acts alone.

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: Autonomy is a setting we choose for each task, not a feature of the technology. The rule: the more independently it acts, the stronger the oversight must be.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Which is where "human in the loop" comes in.

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: Yes. A person reviews or approves at the moments that matter. And for decisions about a worker's benefits, a person decides.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Before we switch something on, how do we know it's good enough?

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: We test it, like any other control. These tests are called evals, short for evaluations. Run it over past claims, with personal details removed, and score it: right answer, sources shown, fair, private, and knows when to hand over to a person.

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: Then keep testing after launch, because models, data and policies change. Test before you trust.

scenes.title: Copilot is the floor, not the ceiling

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: We all have Copilot already. Isn't that our AI strategy?

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: Copilot is the floor, not the ceiling. Give everyone a Copilot and each person gets a bit faster. That's real. But the journey stays the same shape: same handoffs, same waiting.

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: The bigger gains come from redesigning the journey itself, with agents doing the busywork between people, and people at the decisions.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: That's a much bigger change.

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: And history says it's the one that pays. When factories got electricity, most bolted an electric motor onto the old layout, and productivity barely moved for decades. The big gains came when factories were redesigned around the new power.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: How do we tell AI opportunities apart?

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: Think of a ladder. Rung one: personal productivity, like Copilot drafting a letter, owned by each of us. Rung two: team workflow, like medical files summarized for adjudicators, owned by managers.

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: Rung three: an end-to-end journey, like the claim journey redesigned. Rung four: new services, things WCB couldn't do before, like reaching a worker early, before a claim goes long.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And the top two?

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: They cross teams, systems and policy, so only executives can own them. Most organizations stop at rung one. The value is at three and four.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Why not wait until the technology settles down?

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: Because the two move at different speeds. By one independent measure, the length of task an AI agent can complete has been doubling roughly every seven months. Getting ready takes years.

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: Agents depend on foundations: clean, connected data; rules that are written down; identities and access for agents; people with the skills to direct them; owners for each journey; and monitoring, so we can see what an agent did.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: So starting late costs more than the delay.

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: Much more.

scenes.title: What stays human, and the day ahead

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: With all that change, what stays the same?

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: Four things stay with people. Judgment on decisions that affect a worker's life. Empathy for someone who is hurt and worried. Accountability for every decision. And the worker's voice, including the right to ask for a human review.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: In the session, we'll put this to work in three acts. See it: where AI creates value. Choose it: which opportunities to pursue. Govern it: what only executives can do.

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: Bring one question you want answered. And now, the short version, set to music.
